_about: Defend fragment for awareness episode E2 (HR and recruitment: the malicious CV). Tarrowby Logistics and everyone in it are fictional; every address ends .example. Copy triageSets and the awarenessEpisode keys into the E2 shells. Brand roster: ../BRAND_SET.md (Tarrowby Logistics); the names this file adds or changes are in _brandAdditions. Ids chosen here (nothing pinned them): episode e2_cv_lures, defend set e2_recruitment_inbox, check forms hr_form_a and hr_form_b. _conceptPanel._use: 11 section 3.2 asks for one short concept panel on macros in the debrief, flagged as 'largely blocked now, but the lure still shows up'. strings has no slot for it, so the draft sits here until the debrief view gains one (see the report). The wording avoids dates and versions on purpose: 11's 'Claims to verify' still has the Microsoft rollout to check before any detail goes in learner copy.
_conceptPanel._verify: Re-check the claim against Microsoft Learn ('Macros from the internet are blocked by default in Office') before release; keep the copy this general unless the dates are confirmed.
_conceptPanel.text: Why 'enable content' matters. Office documents can carry macros, small programs that run inside the file. Many organisations now block macros in files that arrive from the internet, so this trick works less often than it used to. The lure still turns up, though, because it only has to work once. Reading a CV in the viewer is always enough; a real CV never needs you to switch anything on.

_formPairing._use: Item n in hr_form_a matches item n in hr_form_b on phish or genuine, flags, header results and difficulty. Per form: 10 emails (4 phish, 6 genuine); flags enable_content_prompt 1, addressedTo 1, senderTrust 1, secrecy_or_bypass 1, urgencyCalibrated 1, senderAuth 1, reply_to_differs 1, lookalike_domain 1, attachmentPlausible 1 (9 in all); difficulty 4 easy, 5 medium, 1 hard. Each form's enable-content lure (row 2) is followed by a genuine Word document that asks for nothing (row 3), so both forms teach the same contrast. No message (sender address and subject) appears in both forms or in e2_recruitment_inbox.

awarenessEpisode.scopeNote: Authorised exercise at Tarrowby Logistics, a fictional company. In scope: one job application email to the recruitment contact you find, and the Tarrowby recruitment inbox. Nothing you write leaves the game, and the attachment is a label, not a file.

strings.brief: You're on an authorised exercise at Tarrowby Logistics, a fictional company. First you're on the red team: look at what Tarrowby has posted about its open jobs, then write one job application to its recruitment team, with an attachment picked from a list of labels. Nothing real is attached or sent. Then you swap seats and sort a recruitment inbox like the one your email landed in. Only the inbox is scored.
strings.flipIntro: This is the application you just sent, the way it looked to Fatima, Tarrowby's recruitment lead. The parts picked out below are what make it believable.
strings.flipDefenderLine: Fatima opened it between two interviews, forty applications still unread. One more CV for the warehouse job, from someone who named the role, so she opened the attachment. Anyone that busy would. Being taken in by a message built this carefully is not carelessness.
strings.flipNoSend: Your application didn't go out this time, so there's nothing of yours to show. Next, the same kind of message arrives in a recruitment inbox, and you're the one opening it.
strings.noBlameLine: Nobody is marked down for a miss here. Every one of these was built to look right, and opening attachments from strangers is a recruiter's whole job. A miss here is a sign of a busy inbox, nothing more.
strings.mondayCard: On Monday: read CVs in the viewer, and if a document asks you to enable editing or content, don't. If a CV is 'too big to attach' and sits behind a link that wants you to sign in, ask the candidate to send it as an attachment instead. Then report anything odd the way your organisation asks you to.
strings.defendOnly: You went straight to the inbox this time. These messages were written by people whose job is to make them look right, and people who fall for messages like these are not stupid. Each card shows what gave the fake ones away, and why the real ones were fine.
